prompt: In Raft, what must a node do before it can request votes to start a new election?
choices: Increment its current term number and vote for itself
Decrement its current term number
Wait for an AppendEntries heartbeat from the existing leader
Append a no-op entry to its log

prompt: In the 5-node trace, S3 (leader of term 1) is partitioned off with only S1. Why can S3 not commit the entry 'SET x=3' at index 3?
choices: It cannot get acknowledgment from a majority of the cluster (needs 3 of 5, has only 2)
S1 explicitly rejects the entry as invalid
Term 1 is no longer a valid term number
Index 3 is reserved for configuration changes

prompt: When the partition heals and S4 (term 2 leader) sends AppendEntries to S3, what happens to S3's uncommitted index-3 entry ('SET x=3', term 1)?
choices: It is deleted and overwritten by the leader's entry at that index because the terms conflict
It is merged together with the leader's entry into a single combined command
S3 keeps it and asks the client to retry the commit
It is automatically marked committed since it arrived first

prompt: Per Gilbert and Lynch's formalization of the CAP theorem, which statement is accurate?
choices: During an actual network partition, a system must choose between remaining fully consistent and remaining available; it cannot guarantee both at once
A well-engineered system can always provide consistency, availability, and partition tolerance simultaneously
Partition tolerance is optional and can be designed out of a distributed system
CAP means a system must permanently give up one of the three properties at all times, partition or not

prompt: In the Dynamo shopping-cart example, what is the concrete, client-visible cost of choosing availability over consistency during a partition?
choices: An item the customer previously deleted from the cart can reappear after reconciliation, because divergent versions are merged by union rather than one being discarded
The cart becomes completely read-only until the partition heals
All writes during the partition are rejected with an explicit error to the client
The customer's session is forcibly terminated when the partition is detected

prompt: Using the two-node replicated-counter example, what distinguishes eventual consistency from strong consistency?
choices: Under eventual consistency, a client reading a replica can observe a stale value for some window after a write; under strong consistency, every read anywhere reflects the latest committed write immediately
Eventual consistency guarantees faster reads with no other tradeoff
Strong consistency requires at least five replicas to function
Eventual consistency only applies to counters, not to general key-value data

prompt: What does causal consistency guarantee that plain eventual consistency does not?
choices: Writes that causally depend on an earlier observed value are seen in that dependency order by every node, even though unrelated concurrent writes may still be observed in different orders on different nodes
Every write in the entire system is applied in one single global total order on all nodes
No replica is ever allowed to lag behind another
It requires a single leader node, exactly like strong consistency

prompt: In the GitHub October 2018 incident, Orchestrator's own failover decisions were coordinated via a Raft quorum and worked correctly, yet the incident still caused data divergence. Why?
choices: The underlying MySQL data replication was not itself quorum-based, so promoting a new primary gave no guarantee that every acknowledged write had reached it before the old primary was deposed
Raft requires at least seven nodes to avoid split-brain, and Orchestrator only had three
Raft cannot elect a leader during any network partition, so no failover should have occurred at all
MySQL replication automatically uses the same log format as Raft, so the two systems should have been fully interchangeable
